findings.title: IAM managed policy grants administrative access
findings.description: An Allow statement with Action "*" (or "iam:*") on Resource "*" is administrative access in a customer-managed policy. Scope actions and resources to least privilege.

evidence.actual: Allow statement with Action "*"/"iam:*" on Resource "*"

findings.remediation:
Replace the admin-managed policy attachment with scoped inline or customer-managed
policies (see AEGIS-AWS-006 fix). If break-glass admin access is required, gate it
behind a separate role with MFA condition and CloudTrail alerting:
Condition = { Bool = { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent" = "true" } }

path.detail: any identity attached to this policy gains administrative access

findings.title: IAM policy allows privilege escalation (create policy + attach policy)
findings.description: The policy combines a policy-authoring action (iam:CreatePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:PutGroupPolicy) with a policy-attachment action (iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:AttachGroupPolicy). Attack path: create an administrative policy, attach it to your own role/user, assume full admin. Split authoring from attachment duties and scope each to least privilege.

evidence.actual: Allow statements grant policy-authoring and policy-attachment actions
evidence.expected: separate policy authoring from attachment; scope both to least privilege

findings.remediation:
Split policy authoring from attachment (this combination is the classic privilege
escalation primitive). Remove `iam:CreatePolicy*` / `iam:Attach*Policy` from the
workload policy. Policy management belongs in a separate, human-gated CI/CD role —
never in an application runtime role.

findings.title: IAM permissions management actions allowed on all resources
findings.description: An Allow statement grants IAM write actions (iam:Put*, iam:Create*, iam:Update*, iam:Delete*, iam:Attach*, iam:Detach*, or iam:*) on Resource "*". Attack path: modify any identity's policies directly to escalate to admin. Read-only IAM actions (iam:Get*, iam:List*, iam:Generate*, iam:Simulate*) are excluded. Scope IAM management to specific users, roles, and policies.

evidence.actual: Allow statement grants IAM management action "iam:*" on "*"
evidence.expected: scope IAM management actions to specific identities

findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: Write actions allowed on all resources
findings.description: An Allow statement grants write actions (*:Put*, *:Create*, *:Update*, *:Delete*, *:Modify*) on Resource "*". Attack path: unconstrained writes let an attacker reconfigure, exfiltrate from, or destroy any resource in the account. The blanket Action "*" case is owned by AEGIS-AWS-006. Scope write actions to the resources the workload actually manages.

evidence.actual: Allow statement grants write action "iam:*" on "*"
evidence.expected: scope write actions to specific resources

findings.remediation: Review the flagged configuration against AWS security best practices and the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark. Apply the control the rule describes, preferring restrictive defaults, encryption, and audit logging. Validate with `aegis scan` after the change.

findings.title: IAM privilege chain: workload inherits sensitive actions
findings.description: A workload (EC2, Lambda) assumes an IAM role whose policy grants wildcard or sensitive actions. The chain traces role → policy → workload with evidence at each hop, showing the exact privilege inheritance path an attacker would abuse.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

path.detail: workload assumes role with privileged actions

findings.title: IAM role has no permissions boundary
findings.description: The role sets no permissions_boundary, so nothing caps the maximum permissions its policies can grant — a single overly broad policy attachment becomes fully effective. Set a permissions boundary as a guardrail.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: IAM role has no description
findings.description: The IAM role has no description, so reviewers cannot tell what the role is for or who owns it. Document the role's purpose in the description field.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.

findings.title: IAM policy statement has no Sid
findings.description: At least one policy statement has no Sid, making the statement harder to reference in reviews, audit findings, and exception tracking. Give every statement a descriptive Sid.
findings.remediation: Apply least privilege. Replace wildcard (`*`) actions and resources with the minimum scoped ARNs the workload needs. Split policy authoring from attachment. Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate scoped policies from CloudTrail history.
